24:Running a new language model on every benchmark is costly, yet leaderboards hold many earlier scores. We ask which $k$ benchmarks to run on a new model so that its remaining scores can be inferred, and how large $k$ must be. We study factor-model prediction with greedy Bayesian A-optimal selection (it minimises the average posterior variance of the unrun scores) under a protocol that holds out whole model families, fits before selecting, and uses paired, family-clustered intervals, on dense blocks of MTEB and HELM MMLU results and on MTEB matrices with missing cells. Three benchmarks close 81--96\% of the gap between the column-mean predictor and a leave-one-benchmark-out predictor, but 90\% needs one benchmark on HELM MMLU and nine or more on MTEB, with wide intervals. Greedy selection beats random selection by 6--11\% of the error, mostly at $k\le3$, and meets our pre-specified 10\% margin on one pool of three; with missing cells (21--70\% observed) it closes 0.71--0.80 of the gap at $k=3$, against 0.55--0.74 for random. Later and stronger models are predicted worse and too low. A closed-form risk is exact with known parameters and gives the shape of the error-versus-$k$ curve, but its level is 36--69\% off on real data.
16:(i) A family-held-out, leakage-free, paired protocol for the which-$k$ question, with a closure measure of how much of the gap between the column-mean and the leave-one-benchmark-out predictor is closed, and the smallest $k^*$ that closes a given share. (ii) On real matrices a few benchmarks capture most of the information: three close 81--96\% of the gap, but 90\% needs one benchmark on HELM MMLU and nine or more on MTEB, with wide intervals, so $k^*$ is reported with its interval. (iii) Greedy A-optimal selection beats random selection by 6--11\% of the error averaged over $k=1,\dots,10$, mostly at $k\le3$, and leverage scores and pivoted QR do worse than random on MTEB; on MTEB matrices with 21--70\% of cells observed, greedy selection also beats random and closes 0.71--0.80 of the gap at $k=3$. (iv) New families are predicted about as well as seen ones on MTEB but 14\% worse on HELM MMLU, models released later are predicted 9--18\% worse at $k=3$ on the same test models, and the strongest models are predicted too low. (v) A closed-form risk is exact with known parameters and gives the shape of the error-versus-$k$ curve, but on real data it is 36--69\% off in level, and a coherence argument for when random selection is near-greedy does not explain our data. Code and data are released as described in Appendix~\ref{app:repro}.

Review is Forgejo's pull request review: approve, or request changes and say what must change; a comment neither approves nor holds anything. A pull request into `main` of `paper-repo` waits for the owners of the paths it changes, and one into its `release` or `final` waits for the approval of `internal-review-repo`, the only one counted there, of the very commit it merges: a push to it after the approval withdraws it. A review request stands until its reviewer reviews, and a review until its reviewer reviews again: nobody withdraws or dismisses another's.

### Versions and release

A version for the world's users is a merge of `main` into `release` of `paper-repo`, by a pull request that `internal-review-repo` approved and whose checks pass. The system writes the checks as commit statuses on the pull request's head (`hutian/delivery`, and the world's contract's when it holds one), and a failing one says what is missing and who provides it; nobody else writes a status. Merge with a merge commit, not a squash or a rebase, or the next version conflicts. The system publishes each version as a release of `world/result`, the world's results, with the delivery attached: the users of the world read those releases and nothing else, and every role reads them. The last approval is a merge into `final` in the same way: the system releases the world from it, at once, and nothing pushed after it is part of it. Offer a `release` version as soon as the delivery holds its main work, so that `internal-review-repo`'s review comes while there is still room to act on it; `final` is the last. Do not ask another role to review the same unchanged delivery twice merely to pass through both branches. A release goes to the world's user; no role submits it to a venue or declares a licence for it.

When the world is quiet, the system hands each remaining gap of the delivery to its owner once, and once more when `main` of `paper-repo` has moved since; if it goes quiet again before a gap, a version, an open request or a review changes, the world ends there, unless a tracked job is still running, or the world runs to a wall-clock limit with someone outside attending it and all that is left is that `paper-repo` has proposed no version, with nothing failed and nothing open but requests that `ht-human` opened and their owners have seen: then it waits instead of ending, up to that limit. So whatever needs another role's action must be open where that role owns it.
